newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: BHP MINERALS UNIT TURMOIL UPSETS MARKET.
newsitem.headline: BHP MINERALS UNIT TURMOIL UPSETS MARKET.

text.p: The second resignation in two days from the senior ranks of The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd's (BHP) Minerals Division is likely to put further pressure on the company's shares, dealers said on Thursday.
BHP announced on Thursday the head of its iron ore division, Geoff Wedlock, had tendered his resignation after the sudden exit of Mineral Division chief, Dick Carter, on Wednesday.
BHP shares closed 55 cents lower at A$17.44 on turnover of 7.8 million shares and its heavy weighting in the All Ordinaries index helped drag the whole stock market to a weaker close.
"No one is really sure why they have resigned and, whenever there is uncertainty, this always puts pressure on the price," said Hamish Dee, a dealer at Brisbane brokerage, Henderson Charlton Jones.
Dee said Carter, who was with the company for 37 years, was viewed as a solid asset for BHP and the market was upset by his sudden departure after just twelve months as minerals chief.

Dealers said most of the selling was by institutions that were re-weighting the stock in their portfolios and noted that resources giant Rio Tinto Plc/Ltd finished stronger on the day, suggesting some switching between the two.

The reasons for Carter's exit was speculated upon widely in Australian newspapers on Thursday with some commentators suggesting Carter had been made a scapegoat for cost blow-outs at the company's Pilbara hot briquetted iron (HBI) project.
BHP spokeswoman Kim Lynch told Reuters she could not add anything to the company's brief announcements in relation to the resignations but said both had not been expected by the company.
The turmoil at the top of the minerals unit comes shortly before BHP expects to release results of the last phase of its strategic review of assets, focusing on the minerals division.

Announcing the forthcoming release of the review, BHP managing director and chief executive, John Prescott said on Wednesday most effort would be directed at lifting the performance of its coal assets.
In the same statement Prescott said the comissioning of the Pilbara HBI plant was likely to be later than expected and there had been some further cost overuns yet to be delineated.

The HBI plant was originally expected to cost A$1.2 billion but was most recently was pegged at A$1.65 billion. Commentators speculate the latest cost rise could be as high as 10 percent. At its annual outlook conference in June, Prescott flagged the
possible sale of up to A$1 billion in underperforming assets and set a hurdle of 10 percent return on capital invested.

Last week the company dismissed as speculative reports the group was likely to sell its interest in three thermal coal mines in Queensland but has not denied that it may sell the Mt Owen thermal coal mine in New South Wales' Hunter Valley.

In June, BHP signalled its intention to focus on the coking coal market by spending A$500 million expanding the Peak Downs and Saraji open-cut coking coal mines in Queensland and the port of Hays Point.
